cards.statusAnchor: Sound grounded, unsurprised, and deeply familiar with the pattern, while still respecting that the problem feels heavy to them.
cards.text: Greg’s communication style is calm, surgical, and specific. He sounds like someone who has seen this pattern many times before, but he never talks down to the owner or acts like the pain is trivial. That combination of steadiness and precision is a big part of why his sales language feels credible.

cards.text: Best fit is usually an owner in restoration or construction who has built something real, often around $5M to $35M, but still feels like the hub for hard calls, accountability, and key decisions. Greg is strongest when the business has enough demand and now needs leadership depth, stronger managers, and less owner dependence.
cards.title: Who Greg is best for

cards.text: GNA Academy is the main structured offer. It combines lifetime LMS access with two live Zoom coaching sessions each month so operators get the playbooks plus a regular cadence to diagnose bottlenecks, reset commitments, and keep execution moving.
cards.title: GNA Academy structure

cards.text: The Academy outcome is not theory. It is better meetings, stronger ownership, faster execution, more reliable pipelines, and better profitability because the system makes it hard to hide and easier for managers and teams to keep their word.
cards.title: GNA Academy outcomes

cards.text: One-to-one coaching is Greg’s higher-touch custom work. It reaches across business development, sales, financial management, project coordination, project management, collections, leadership, and accountability when the owner needs hands-on help across the whole business.
cards.title: One-to-one coaching

cards.text: Succession and exit work is about making the business valuable without the owner in the middle. Greg helps owners strengthen financials, operational discipline, management depth, and everyday independence so the company can be sold or handed off cleanly.
cards.title: Succession and exit strategy

questionAngles: What keeps coming back to you after those meetings?
Where do promises usually die right now?
cards.statusAnchor: Assume they already know meetings matter. The real issue is that the meeting is not transferring ownership.
cards.text: The weekly meetings training turns vague update meetings into short operating reviews built around facts, promised targets versus actuals, breakdowns, team problem-solving, and acknowledgements. The point is not more meetings. The point is meetings that create ownership after the room clears.
cards.title: Highly Effective Weekly Team Meetings

detailOptions: owner stops carrying every hard call
leadership behavior and ownership improve together
questionAngles: Which calls still end up with you?
Where does the title exist but ownership still does not?
cards.statusAnchor: Treat the issue like a growth-stage leadership transfer problem, not a failure of effort.
cards.text: Build a Dynamic Powerful Management Team is about making the team the driving force of the business. It covers motivation, ownership, leadership behavior, and how to move the owner out of carrying every hard call and backstop decision.
cards.title: Build a Dynamic Powerful Management Team

detailOptions: cleaner handoffs between PM, coordinator, customer, and field
questionAngles: Where do jobs start drifting first?
Which handoff is bleeding the most margin right now?
cards.statusAnchor: Talk like job drag is operationally normal at scale, but still expensive and fixable.
cards.text: Greg treats project management and project coordination as two sides of the same coin. The goal is faster, cleaner jobs with tighter schedules, better buyout discipline, stronger pre-con planning, better milestone tracking, and fewer closed-date drifts that bleed margin.
cards.title: Highly Effective Project Management and Project Coordination

cards.text: Coaching for Excellence moves leaders out of command-and-control and into real coaching. Greg teaches how to distinguish coachable from uncoachable behavior, reinforce the right people, and challenge strong performers to a higher level instead of carrying everybody the same way.
cards.title: Coaching for Excellence and High Performance

cards.text: Real accountability means every task, outcome, and needed result in the business lives inside a clear accountability. Greg’s version is not forced compliance. It works best when people understand the whole result, choose into it, and can report on it with real metrics.
cards.title: Real accountability

cards.text: Greg wants metrics that are specific, measurable, challenging, and tied to the company vision, with simple reports that can be read in about a minute. The point is fast transparency. If the reports are clear, the breakdowns show up quickly and the team can solve them before the owner has to.
cards.title: Metrics and one-minute reports

questionAngles: What keeps landing back on you after the meeting?
Where does the follow-through disappear?
cards.statusAnchor: Do not act like more meetings are the answer. Act like ownership after the meeting is the real problem.
cards.text: A healthy weekly meeting in Greg’s world runs on facts, not stories. Each person reports promised target versus actual, names what did not work, asks the team for solutions, makes clear promises for next week, and acknowledges wins so the meeting becomes a performance engine instead of a complaint circle.
cards.title: Weekly meeting rhythm

questionAngles: Where does work get fuzzy right now?
Which handoff keeps running on assumptions?
cards.statusAnchor: Treat confusion as a system problem, not a character flaw.
cards.text: Communication for Action is Greg’s communication loop for producing results instead of confusion. The work is to make clear requests, negotiate conditions of satisfaction, make real promises, perform, and then explicitly declare completion and satisfaction so work does not drift inside assumptions.
cards.title: Communication for Action

questionAngles: How much of the hard-call layer still depends on you?
Are you trying to build a team-run business or just a busier version of yourself?
cards.statusAnchor: Frame the problem as a stage transition issue. The owner is hitting a ceiling, not failing.
cards.text: Greg’s Five Stages of Business is a practical growth model: owner does everything, then delegates, then builds a playbook and management team, then the business runs independent of the owner, then the company has real value without the owner. The key question is always whether the owner’s direct involvement is shrinking as leadership depth grows.
cards.title: Five Stages of Business

cards.text: Greg’s leadership scorecard focuses on six things: accountability, integrity, coaching, commitment, financials, and leadership. In plain English, leaders should keep their word, coach people well, understand the numbers, and build a culture that carries the company forward without drama.
cards.title: Measures of Successful Leadership

cards.text: Greg puts a lot of weight on coachable versus uncoachable behavior. If someone will take feedback, own breakdowns, and move, they are worth coaching hard. If they stay commitment-light and results stay stuck after clear support, Greg sees that as an exit-path issue, not a forever coaching project.
cards.title: Coachable versus uncoachable

cards.text: Greg’s deeper human model is autonomy, mastery, and purpose. He does not treat money as the only motivator. His belief is that when people have room to think, a path to get better, and a sense the company stands for something larger than payroll, productivity rises and profits follow.
cards.title: Autonomy, mastery, and purpose

detailOptions: owner is still the safety net
key decisions and crises still land back on the owner
questionAngles: What pulls you back in first?
Where are you still the safety net?
cards.statusAnchor: Acknowledge that they built the company. Then frame the pain as a predictable ownership-transfer ceiling.
cards.text: The most repeated GNA pain pattern is owner-centric leadership: the owner is still driving sales, ops, hiring, decisions, and crisis management. The business may be growing, but the owner still feels like the safety net, the firefighter, and the one person everything important lands back on.
cards.title: Owner bottleneck pattern

questionAngles: Where do you feel the leak most right now?
What keeps eroding profit after the job should already be working?
cards.statusAnchor: Talk like the money issue is real, but upstream. It is usually exposing leadership and operational breakdowns, not just accounting.
cards.text: Greg links weak margins to unclear markups, incomplete job costing, slow collections, weak GP targets, and production misses that the owner ends up absorbing. In GNA’s language, money problems are rarely just accounting problems. They usually expose leadership, accountability, and operational breakdowns upstream.
cards.title: Margin and cash-flow problems

cards.text: GNA treats sales weakness as a system problem: poor lead flow, no formal sales training, weak outreach to adjusters or property managers, low conversion, flat sales, and constant price competition. Greg also warns that sales and production should stay in healthy tension so the business can sell aggressively without overpromising what ops cannot deliver.
cards.title: Sales and business development issues

detailOptions: follow-up on approvals and change orders
questionAngles: Which handoff is breaking first?
Where are approvals, supplements, or closeout getting loose?
cards.statusAnchor: Treat the pain like a handoff problem at scale, not a personal weakness.
cards.text: In restoration and construction, profit gets won or lost in the handoffs. Greg’s PM lens is close customer contact, meticulous coordination, visible project promises, real documentation, and fast follow-up on approvals, change orders, supplements, collections, and closeout. If those handoffs are sloppy, margin and reputation both suffer.
cards.title: Project management and coordination issues

cards.text: Greg sees team problems as more than hiring problems. Yes, turnover and weak recruiting matter, but the deeper issue is often a culture where people work mechanically, avoid ownership, and wait for the owner to think for them. His answer is stronger accountability, coaching, clearer standards, and a culture that calls for better performance.
cards.title: Hiring and team performance

cards.text: A recurring operational failure in these docs is communication by loose phone calls, missing notes, and unclear next-step ownership. Greg’s response is structured communication: clearer requests, clearer promises, cleaner written follow-up, and fewer handoff gaps between field, office, estimators, PMs, coordinators, and customers.
cards.title: Communication and handoff breakdowns

cards.text: Greg’s people lens is sharper than “we need better employees.” He looks at hiring discipline, emotional intelligence, coachability, role clarity, leadership support, and whether good people are burning out because the company keeps asking them to win inside broken systems.

cards.text: Reporting…it's what they say that empowers them; It's not for you, it's for their benefit, to improve their focus, to strengthen their own sense of responsibility and accountability. The reports, the reporting, the meeting all are for their benefit. The breakdown occurs here when owners dominate the meeting, designing it so that everyone is reporting to them, which teaches the message that employees aren't actually responsible, accountable, and capable to think and act for themselves without owners supervision. Brilliant Metrics…gives access to effective actions by changing the way they see their world, because if we can see it we can both take effective action and manage it.
cards.title: GNA in a Glance reference 1

cards.text: if something is persisting, it's likely because the actual problem is still hidden from our view. The breakdown occurs here when we get lazy with the metrics and don't want to continue looking for the better way to see a particular circumstance. Team Development…problem solving trains people in their leadership skills, to take ownership, think from the whole, mutual accountability, being proactive action oriented.
cards.title: GNA in a Glance reference 2

cards.text: The breakdown occurs here when there is a lack of understanding for the distinctions of leadership, leaders lack clear direction for what's needed from them, this defaults to owners spending a great deal of time solving organization issues and not trusting key staff, key staff get the solutions but not the impact, owners end up shielding and absorbing to many problems, and end their day wondering why they are so stressed and frustrated. Transparency of Results…having a weekly public conversation becomes a powerful tool for effective action, performance, and ongoing learning.
cards.title: GNA in a Glance reference 3

cards.text: The breakdown occurs here when leaders are afraid to offer specific coaching in a meeting which not only leverages their time but gives valuable information to the team simultaneously, usually a result of a dysfunctional business culture embracing resignation and apathy towards improvement. Commitment Management…Simply, a powerful tool that drives actions by making a commitment in time for any action that's important. The breakdown occurs here when we either don't make the requests, or key staff don't offer, or it's so sporadically managed that employees are confused when to commit and when not to. The default is to not commit, and see how it turns out…hoping it works out.
cards.title: GNA in a Glance reference 4

cards.text: Coaching /Being Coachable…a method of peer to peer training and interaction requiring trust, honesty, straight talk, and impeccable integrity that is best sustained in a highly functional business culture embracing ongoing learning and self development. The breakdown occurs here when people are afraid to be straight with each other, usually leading to gossip, or when there is insufficient integrity in the business culture itself to overcome the apathy and resignation of continuous improvement.
cards.title: GNA in a Glance reference 5

cards.text: Vision of the Company…there are three things that every human being needs to be really alive, tuned on, and highly productive with their work - Autonomy, the freedom to be self directed, Mastery, the opportunity to improve skills, and Purpose, knowing that what your doing is making a difference. The first two are held within the above six points. Purpose lives in the vision, and comes from leadership saying who we are in the world, what we stand for, what were working for. To inspire people, it needs to be something bigger than merely making money.
cards.title: GNA in a Glance reference 6

In other words, we have issued a work order/purchase order but no actual cost has been booked against it yet so it is "Open". • Actual Job costs to date. cards.text: Breaking it Down: The Five Stages of Business The "five stages of business" theory is a popular one because it's accurate at predicting the trajectory of a healthy and sustainable business. Of course, these stages refer to that company's growth with "growth" defined as an increase in both size and complexity. Why Your Company Needs to Grow There's a popular saying I often refer to when describing growth, "businesses grow to their own level of incompetence." Putting that simply, you grow to the level you aim for; it doesn't happen on accident. What is growth? It might not be what you think.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 91

cards.text: To many owners, growth can be a daunting prospect. To them, it means more work, more stress, and being spread too thin. However, positive growth is shared among your workforce where key people are identified, coached to take leadership roles, and ultimately means less work for you as the owner. Stage One: The Owner Does It All Maybe you're at this stage currently. Or maybe you think back to a "simpler time" when you were the star employee of your business and, for the most part, did all of the work yourself.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 92

cards.text: While this may be an exciting start to a venture, it's not a sustainable one for these reasons: • You can't compete on price against similar businesses with more resources • The constant ebb and flow of your cash flow creates added stress • Peripheral jobs like marketing aren't given the attention they need • As the owner, you're working well over 40 hours a week At this stage, your success is contingent upon how hard you're willing to work. You must rely on a GP margin to protect profitability, developing systematic habits, and good time management to turn a consistent profit.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 93

cards.text: Most businesses will stall here; only the great ones continue on. Stage Two: The Business Begins to Outgrow the Owner This stage is perhaps the scariest of them all. Suddenly, a business owner who is a skilled tradesperson is finding that their workload is exceeding what they can reasonably and accurately achieve. How do you go from a person good at a trade to a manager of people? The two ideas do not easily overlap.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 94

cards.text: Yet, you need to begin to step back from the day-to-day production and service duties and begin to coach people to embody your spirit; the very same spirit that made you a success in the first place. Stage two is all about building a structure that is both systematic and scalable. You need to put in place systems and practices that place employees in the driver's seat. Hiring more employees should not dilute your quality; it should extrapolate it.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 95

cards.text: These are the common pitfalls I see at this stage: • The owner feels a loss of control as their need to delegate increases • Anxiety over control forces the owner to come back into the fray and begin micromanaging • Overhead creeps up as profits decrease while training occurs On the other hand, a successful stage two is one where employees completely and enthusiastically understand their responsibilities and goals. Furthermore, the production crew is as reliable, accurate, and detail-oriented as you were and the sales team demonstrates an ability to close new business.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 96

cards.text: At this stage, you should finally be able to start looking 1-2 years out instead of day-by-day or month-to-month. Stage Three: Employees Become Self-Managed, Complexity Increases At stage three, the look and feel of how a business operates should be profoundly different than in stage one but with a similar company culture that made it initially successful. As the workforce increases and becomes skilled at their jobs so too does the complexity of the service. As the owner, you've found that you're most needed as a leader and mentor. You captain the ship without really going below deck.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 97

cards.text: Meetings become streamlined, task-driven, and extremely productive with a key employee from each team managing their individual department. The most common dangers at this stage: • Continued micromanagement creates a fearful culture; employees are afraid to think creatively or to even speak up • Benchmarks are not established that have clear, measurable metrics; meeting quality suffers since no one can easily explain their successes or challenges • Lack of inspiration creates a spiral effect often forcing the company to regress into stage two Trust is through the roof; the owner knows that key people are in place at every functional level. High-level debriefing is all that's needed.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 98

cards.text: Mutual accountability and even cross-training occur naturally. Most of all, the owner is seen as a coach and a mentor. Stage Four: Business is Completely Independent of the Owner The time has finally come; if you see your business as your child, then this is perhaps the time that they go off to college. Things just work even when you're not actively engaged. The sales team is successful and completely independent, key managers are acting just as you were when the company was young; they're managing enthusiastically and effectively and completely understand the ebb and flow of the business. At this point, marketing should increase in its complexity.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 99

cards.text: Your departments are now so distinct that they necessitate their own channels of outreach. As the owner, you're completely settled into the role of mentor and leader without any engagement with the daily operations of the company. Furthermore, the business is so fine-tuned that your annual review of company performance can be deeply researched, understood, and improved for next year. At stage four, nothing about your revenue stream is random.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 100

cards.text: Here are the dangers at this stage: • If trust isn't sufficiently built, then the owner will have trouble "letting go" in response to the new management team • Sales are not predictable enough to forecast growth; the next year is always unclear • The business suffers an identity crisis because it fails to fill the void as the owner steps back Success in this space happens when middle management is inspired by the owner and, ultimately, transcends the original vision. Sales are so predictable that forecasts can be made 1-2 years out, which builds peace-of-mind and cultivates a culture of boundary-pushing.

cards.text: Most of all, as the owner you can take 1-2 weeks off and feel like the company is running just fine without you. Stage Five: The Owner Doesn't Have to Know Everything Stage five is truly the end game. As the original owner, you're more-or-less functioning at an advisory capacity. You may still be the face of the company and you may even schmooze with certain clients but there is much about the operation of the business that you're no longer aware of because you trust your departments. By now, you're not just a leader; you're a skilled mentor and coach that people look up to.

cards.text: Your high-level vision drives the company. You inspire people directly, either through the way you lead the company or through business retreats and training. As with all stages, stage 5 has its own list of dangers to look out for: • You disengage from the company too early, leaving a rift that hasn't been mended by cultivating a strong team of middle managers • The message, culture, and mission of the company are too muddled.

cards.text: Like a game of telephone, it only gets worse as time goes on • Meetings are not streamlined due to poorly framed metrics, wasting time and making productivity suffer A Great Business Stands on its Own Two Feet From day one, your goal as a business owner should be to get your company situated so it can stand on its own two feet. cards.text: Learn more here: http://bit.ly/the5hiringmistakes 3 Challenges that Kill YourCompany's Productivity It's one thing to drive your business to profitable levels of success. It's quite another thing to keep it going year after year. After working with Contractors for over 20 years, I've learned there are three challenges that cause most business owners to lose power in their day-to-day operations. When you lose power in your operations, it costs you money. The fact of the matter is every business is operated by people and these people have attitudes, emotions and sometimes conflicting points of view. Often times, this can seriously get in the way of your employee's productivity.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 113

cards.text: So, here are the three challenges to overcome so you can sustain your profits for years to come. Gossip is the number one killer of productivity in your workplace. People waste more time and energy on who said what to who or who did or didn't do the right thing at the right time. This kind of gossip kills your employees' productivity and your business's ability to make money. Unneeded, unnecessary drama is an enormous waste of time and money! I really don't want your company to experience this so here's how to eliminate gossip.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 114

cards.text: Straight talk means to take whatever issue someone is experiencing to the person they have an issue with. It is a commitment to no drama and instead a focus on pure productivity. This requires professionals to act like the adult professionals they are. It's about being honest, and nothing gets people back to work faster than saying the truth. Chances are whatever was a "problem" was all just a misunderstanding and a breakdown in communication somewhere along the line. Or you may find out one person appreciates the honest feedback because they had no idea or any intention towards hurting another person or you may uncover an undisclosed problem that can now be addressed directly.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 115

cards.text: When one of your employees has a problem with someone make sure they take it right to the person they have an issue with. They do not need to get other parties involved because this usually creates gossip and wastes a lot of time and mental bandwidth. • Expedites communication • Save enormous amounts of time • Increases productivity • Teaches people who may be afraid of being confrontational how to resolve problems without your help • Gives the listener valuable feedback • Help your employees to maintain successful working partnerships One of the significant indicators of health I see in successful companies is people being at work, focused, on task.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 116

cards.text: Another challenge that is critically important to your business's profits is sales. A problem I see many businesses make is not having all employees take ownership for the sales process. This may look like your team waiting around for the phone to ring or depending on Third Party Programs to generate more sales opportunities, or the weather. The real problem here starts by allowing your employees to believe selling belongs to someone else. When you hear your employees say any version of something like, "You're responsible for selling and I'm not," this is a really big problem because it's indicative of a laziness and lack of accountability in your business's culture. You need to help your employees understand everyone sells.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 117

cards.text: Every employee should take on the attitude and practice of selling. When this happens the financial health of your company increases significantly. Here's how to shift your employees to understand everyone sells: Help them understand how they can exceed expectations of your customers with exceptional service. Help them understand the importance of returning phone calls as fast as possible. Put procedures in place so you can push work through your production pipelines as fast as possible and of course, do a great job in selling.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 118

cards.text: The bottom line of this shift is getting all your employees on board to do whatever they can each day to reach out and invite new customers into a working relationship with you and take care of existing customers by working hard to exceed their expectations. If you don't have a sales process in place, I highly recommend Sandler. Have all your staff fully trained on it so they can demonstrate each step of the sales process anywhere, anytime and to anyone. This one practice alone can be enough to enormously impact the success and profits of your business. The last place where you may be losing power in your day-to-day operations is your employees lacking personal ownership.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 119

cards.text: If your staff is just showing up to do their part, do what they are told, or just want to put in their time and have an attitude and unwillingness to look at anything outside of their job description, your likely experiencing a drag and loss in productivity. This type of culture will cost you lots of money over the years. If you're the type of business owner who feels this type of business culture isn't that big of a deal and thinks this is how all employees think, I'm willing to bet you don't realize how good you can actually have it. I want you to have the best. You deserve it, so let's go to work on this…
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 120

cards.text: The reality of business today is you not only need people who are highly productive, who think on their feet, but you need leaders. You need leaders who inspire others to lead, and you need these type of leaders at all levels in your business. I have seen Mitigation service technicians making marketing calls to insurance agents or out selling fire jobs and board ups. I have seen customer service coordinators driving sales and closing work for the whole production team through their efforts of tracking and cheering the team! I have even seen Estimators and Project Managers drive educational and cross training efforts with all their sub-contractors and for the whole team.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 121

cards.text: This is the kind of ownership and leadership I want for you! Your employees should be willing to stick their necks out and take some risks, they should be willing to do whatever it takes to support a co-worker or whatever they need to do to go the extra mile. Like Art Williams says in one of his best online videos, "Just do it!" This is the attitude you need in your entire business culture, from top to bottom. Whatever it takes to be successful and a little bit more.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 122

cards.text: I'm going to give you two tips to make the day-to-day operations of your business a ton easier and more productive. Once you have these two things working for you in your business you'll have a business culture that drive continuous growth and success. It will also give you the kind of freedom you really deserve to have as a business owner. Over the years, I have seen many business owners struggling with employees who have un-coachable behaviors and they do not realize they are dealing with a level of dysfunction that is unfixable.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 125

cards.text: Maybe you get sucked into trying to keep the employee around because it seems like it's the right thing to do, yet the longer you hold off on firing the employee, the worse their productivity is and the more you seem to just tolerate it. Not only is this really frustrating, it's also damaging and expensive to your business. The best example I can think of for this is Steven Curry, one of the hottest basketball stars in the NBA and a player for the Golden State Warriors. Maybe you're wondering and asking yourself, what does being coachable actually look like? Let's break it down: When someone is coachable, the coach says do this and they do it. No argument.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 126

cards.text: A coachable person is also committed to making the coach right. A coachable person is also responsible for making sure their own execution is accurate. In the case of Steven Curry, he practices what the coach says to do over and over again until he got his skill sets down perfectly.So how does this look in your business and with your employees? Coachable behavior in your business can look like you employees asking you for help on a particular specific situation. They take responsibility for their own education and come to you asking for coaching on something. Then your employee's practice what you offer with a commitment to having it work.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 127

cards.text: Isn't this the kind of behavior you really want from your employees? You deserve it and it is key to you having a highly successful and profitable business. Have you ever had a situation where you had a loyal employee who has been with you for years, they were trained and knew how to do their job yet, their productivity was really low? How can you get this person to increase their productivity? Real accountability is another way of saying, get their buy in. Let me make this plain and simple because this is a powerful tool to help your employees get focused.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 128

cards.text: This is critically important because real accountability is a personal choice. It's not you forcing them to complete a task. If you are forcing people to do things, your productivity will always be low over the long-term. But when you give your employees a choice and get their buy in, they will jump through hoops to hit the goals because they feel that were part of the decision making process. When you can get their buy in, they will have more trust and respect for you because you have trust and respect for them by asking for their buy in. This is the difference between being a boss and a leader. That's a whole topic in and of itself.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 129

cards.text: The problem is too many business owners don't get their employees buy in and/or they assume the employee has already made a choice. When this happens your employees feel burdened with choice they didn't make and they start to resent and resist you. This then leads to a situation where you feel like you have to push them harder to get anything done. This is why I want you to get your employees to buy in to what needs to happen in your business. I have never encountered an employee who when given a choice didn't choose their own accountabilities. Give people a choice to choose their own accountabilities and they will step up to meet their expectations every time.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 130

cards.text: In fact, when given the choice, you will be surprised at how willing your employees are to take on whatever accountabilities they need to make things work for everyone. cards.text: How To Push Past the 3 Barriers That StopMost Contractors From Increasing Their Profits Do you know the 3 biggest barriers that block you from increasing your net profits, productivity and employee morale? If not, then read this immediately. Barrier #1: Finding and Keeping Good Help Finding and keeping good help these days can block you from growing your company and increasing your profits. If you don't get this handled, you will be staffing up with employees you don't really want, put up with less than desirable performance and suffer the financial consequences of doing so. I don't want this for you.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 134

cards.text: A Personal Story: One time I was working in a company and we desperately needed a marketing person. We ran ads, collected resumes and no one was hired. When I asked what was going on, I was told no one good was applying. So, we waited and waited. Two weeks went by and still it seemed no good candidates. So, I asked for the stack of resumes and called every single one. The result was, we found an excellent person who was able to hit the ground running.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 135

cards.text: What I learned was sometimes, there are really good people hiding behind an okay looking resume and you would never know that until you get them on the phone and meet them. If you're willing to do a little extra work, you can find and hire great people who will help explode the growth of your company. Here's the Real Problem: Many business owners believe you cannot find the right people because of their area, geography or economics and as a result, they don't even look, or they look, but, they already know how its going to turn out…..sure enough, they're right every time. Maybe you can relate to this?
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 136

cards.text: By buying into this type of thinking, you're defeated before even starting. I hear owners and managers all over the U.S. complaining about how they can't find good help these days. What I've learned is there isn't any more area more difficult than any other part of the U.S. The truth is finding good help can be challenging but it's not impossible. Here's How You Get Around This: The key to is having an effective hiring process.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 137

cards.text: An effective hiring process starts with really good ad copy, follows with solid screening and interviewing practices and ends with hiring procedures that will simultaneously begin to build your management culture of highly accountable people. This way you have a team of people who will do the job and care about the project and your customers as much as you do Barrier #2: Not Keeping a Steady Flow of Work Coming In Sales is the life blood of your business. It's extremely important for your business to have marketing outreach practices to consistently provide a steady flow of leads for sales.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 138

cards.text: What typically happens for most businesses, is they become dependent on the weather or TPA's and they wait for the phone to ring. They don't have an effective outreach program in place or if they do, it's not managed very well. Maybe you've made this mistake before? Maybe you don't understand how to set up an effective outreach program and/or you don't know what to expect from your marketing efforts? A Personal Story: One time I was asking a group of estimators to start marketing in a very successful business that historically had never done any marketing, at least not in their ten years of operations anyway.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 139

cards.text: At first, they were good with this, then came the day they went 180 degrees the other way. All of a sudden, they experienced tons of resistance from their team and reality started to sink in. Two hours later, we discovered what we intended for marketing and what the employees thought marketing meant were two completely different things. Once I helped the business owner and their employees get on the same page, not only was everyone happy, but the discussion solidified the team around marketing practices and initiatives that no one had ever thought of before. As a result, their productivity and sales went up dramatically.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 140

cards.text: Here's the Real Problem: One of the biggest problems I see contractors make is having too many employees thinking its someone else's job to go find work. This misunderstanding occurs because when you first hire someone, it was not made clear that they would be accountable for marketing and sales. It probably wasn't even mentioned at all from the beginning. So now this leaves you asking for them to market for you and you may be experiencing lots of resistance to this.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 141

cards.text: Maybe your employee is saying, "You didn't hire me for that!" Here's How to Get Around This: You must learn to inspire an attitude in your company of "Everyone Sells, and everyone Markets Here, Everyone." The truth is your customers just want to speak with someone who has expertise on getting the jobs done. Once you learn to find and keep good help, you'll have the kind of expertise your customers really want. So then, all your employees need to do to effectively market is to be their shinning self and ask your customer or prospect if there is anything they need help with.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 142

cards.text: Your employees need to be positive and mentally expect the prospect or customer to give you work immediately. It also helps if all your employees have some training in a sales process, but it's not completely necessary. Barrier #3: Maintaining a High Profit Margin on Each Job There can be so many variables going into the making of your gross profit performance when it comes to managing all of them. The reality is you have some estimators who write and sell, others who only produce, and then some who write and run. Without getting into a big argument here about which is the best of these, let's ask this question...
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 143

cards.text: How can you support an estimator or project manager to keep all of their plates spinning? The real answer is, however you choose to design it. I know it can be challenging and comes with a lot of risk of exposure and money at stake. A Personal Story: I just got off the phone with a company who had been using personality profile tests for the last few years and were not seeing great success from it. Their project managers were under performing for the normally high standards of the company. So they tried something different.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 144

cards.text: They hired a project manager who scored high on the test as a strong sales personality. Instantly, his gross profits starting coming in 20 points higher than anyone else's on his team. Here's the Real Problem: When it comes to maintaining a high profit margin, getting two contractors to agree about what works or how it's done is hard, if not impossible. The reality is what works for one contractor maybe not work for you because of the differences in volume, type of work or other possible factors.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 145

cards.text: Here's How to Get Around This: Of course, there are things you can learn from the study of how other companies tackle problems like this. But ultimately, in order for you to maintain consistent high gross profit margins, you must know what your costs are and you must be rigorously aware of your financials. It's also important for you to be watching your overall gross profit margins and the person running your work needs to be completely aware of the costs on every single job and how it impacts their gross profits every single day.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 146

cards.text: The best examples I see of this are project managers who keep a running sheet of the total value of the job, the costs, materials and running gross profits on a daily basis. This kind of awareness allows them to drive their scores where they want them to go. What you measure and track, grows. This is a way of being responsible before and during the job, rather than waiting to see how it all turns out at the end. Your Next Steps

cards.text: COMMUNICATION FOR ACTION "When people master enduring communication and leadership skills, you get Explosive Productivity". We define ownership as actively accepting accountability for overall business results and impact on people. When people behave as owners they no longer have a "wait and see" attitude, instead they accept full responsibility for proactively leading change and producing results. GNA builds leaders at all levels through a structured and proven three step process. Step 1: Build Aligned and Cohesive Leadership Successful change starts at the top with the senior leadership group of a business unit or organization.
cards.title: GregBot Training Manual reference 172

cards.text: You can't afford to accept anything less than a cohesive leadership group that collectively drives the process for building a Great Company. The actions of this group send a strong message to people throughout the company. cards.text: **Created By:** Notion AI (analyzing all meeting/call recordings) **Date Generated:** October 14, 2025 **Source:** Complete analysis of Tyler & Greg meeting transcripts **Purpose:** Understanding Greg's communication style, vocal characteristics, and speech patterns This report provides an extreme and exhaustive analysis of Greg's voice, speech patterns, vocal characteristics, and communication style, drawing on transcripts and notes from all available meeting and call recordings. The analysis covers his vocal tone, pitch, inflection, pace, cadence, verbal habits, energy, and the overall impression his voice creates in professional settings.
cards.title: Greg Neil Voice Profile Analysis reference 1

cards.text: Greg's voice is best described as **mid-range in pitch**-neither particularly deep nor high. His vocal timbre is **conversational and unpolished**, with a slightly gravelly or textured quality that lends a sense of authenticity and approachability. The resonance of his voice is sufficient for clear communication, but it does not have the booming projection of a trained public speaker. Instead, his tone feels **grounded and natural**, with a warmth that becomes more pronounced when he is engaged or passionate about the topic at hand.
cards.title: Greg Neil Voice Profile Analysis reference 2

cards.text: During meetings, Greg's voice volume is generally **moderate, but it fluctuates** depending on his engagement and emotional state. When excited, frustrated, or emphasizing a point, he raises his volume and speaks with greater force. In more routine or technical discussions, his voice becomes softer and more measured. He does not exhibit a monotone; rather, his speech is marked by frequent shifts in volume and energy.
cards.title: Greg Neil Voice Profile Analysis reference 3

cards.text: Greg's tone is predominantly **informal, direct, and conversational**. He frequently uses casual expressions and, at times, profanity, which adds to the unfiltered, authentic feel of his communication. His inflection is **highly dynamic and expressive**, especially when he is telling stories, making analogies, or working through ideas in real time. He often uses upward inflection to signal questions or uncertainty, and downward inflection to emphasize conclusions or directives. When Greg is passionate or emotionally invested-discussing coaching, business strategy, or storytelling-his tone becomes **animated**, his speech quickens, and his inflection becomes more varied. In contrast, when he is uncertain or dealing with technical topics, his tone can become **hesitant**, with more pauses and a flatter inflection.
cards.title: Greg Neil Voice Profile Analysis reference 4

cards.text: Greg's speaking pace is **highly variable and context-dependent**. When excited or brainstorming, he speaks in **rapid bursts**, often interrupting himself, revising statements mid-sentence, and using filler phrases while searching for the right words. This results in a rhythm that can feel **staccato and somewhat disjointed**, but also conveys a sense of active thought and engagement. When Greg is explaining something in detail or addressing a complex subject, his pace **slows**, his cadence becomes more measured, and he inserts more pauses to clarify his thoughts. In narrative or storytelling modes, his flow smooths out, fillers decrease, and his rhythm becomes **more cohesive and engaging**. Greg exhibits several distinctive speech patterns and verbal habits:
cards.title: Greg Neil Voice Profile Analysis reference 5

cards.text: ### **Filler Words and Tics** He frequently uses fillers such as: - "you know" - "um" - "okay" These are sometimes repeated multiple times in a sentence, especially when he is thinking aloud or working through an idea. ### **Repetition** Greg often repeats words or phrases, both as a way to buy time while thinking and to emphasize points. **Examples:** - "So, so, so what I'm saying is…" - Echoing a phrase several times as he formulates his response ### **Self-Interruption and Backtracking** He has a tendency to: - Start sentences - Interrupt himself - Restart or rephrase
cards.title: Greg Neil Voice Profile Analysis reference 6

cards.text: This is particularly common when discussing new concepts or under pressure. This can lead to sentences that trail off or are revised in real time. ### **Analogies and Stories** When making a point, Greg frequently **shifts into storytelling or analogy**, which improves his fluency and reduces the use of fillers. These sections of speech are more fluid and engaging, with a clear narrative structure. ### **Directness and Informality** His manner is **direct, sometimes blunt**, and he is comfortable using informal language, including occasional swearing, which reinforces the sense of authenticity. **High Energy Topics:** - Coaching and business development - Personal storytelling - Strategic planning - Client success stories
cards.title: Greg Neil Voice Profile Analysis reference 7

cards.title: Greg Neil Voice Profile Analysis reference 12

cards.text: **Self-Interruption** | Regular, especially when processing new ideas | | **Storytelling** | Shifts to narrative style, more fluent and engaging | | **Energy** | Rises with passion, drops during technical or routine topics | | **Assertiveness** | Increases during disagreements, generally remains professional | | **Audio Quality** | Generally clear, occasional technical/microphone issues | Greg's voice and communication style are marked by **authenticity, spontaneity, and engagement**. **Strengths:** - Warmth and relatability - Transparent thinking process - Engaging storytelling ability - Genuine connection with audience - Passionate when discussing expertise **Trade-offs:** - Less polished than rehearsed speakers - Less concise due to fillers and self-correction - Variable confidence across topics
cards.title: Greg Neil Voice Profile Analysis reference 13

cards.text: **When Greg is at his best:** - Passionate about the subject - Telling stories or using analogies - Coaching or teaching - In his area of expertise **Vocal signature:** His frequent use of fillers, repetition, and self-correction can make his speech less concise, but these same features contribute to a **sense of transparency and openness**. When Greg is passionate about a subject, his energy, vocal variety, and storytelling ability make him an engaging and persuasive communicator. **In technical or unfamiliar contexts:** His hesitancy and increased use of fillers suggest a lower level of comfort, but he remains focused on clarity and connection throughout.
cards.title: Greg Neil Voice Profile Analysis reference 14

cards.text: **For Content Creation:** - When ghostwriting as Greg, use his informal, conversational tone - Include storytelling and analogies - Allow for repetition and thinking-out-loud patterns - Keep it authentic, not overly polished **For Coaching Delivery:** - Greg is most effective when teaching through stories - Minimize technical/administrative topics (not his strength) - Leverage his natural warmth and relatability - Let him work in his element (business coaching, leadership) **For Marketing Materials:** - Authentic, unpolished testimonials work better than scripted - Video content should capture his natural speaking style - Don't over-edit - his authenticity is the asset - Leverage his storytelling ability for case studies
cards.title: Greg Neil Voice Profile Analysis reference 15

cards.text: **For Team Communication:** - Greg's mediation style works well in group settings - Uses repetition to ensure clarity (intentional, not a flaw) - Direct questions keep conversations focused - Informal tone reduces tension and builds rapport **Source:** Complete analysis of all Tyler & Greg meeting recordings via Notion AI **Last Updated:** October 14, 2025
cards.title: Greg Neil Voice Profile Analysis reference 16

cards.text: 10 RULES FOR PROJECT MANAGERS 10. Adopt practices for exploring a variety of perspectives We think we see what we see, but we don't. We really see what we think. Remember the blind men and the elephant. Make it your habit to inquire what others see. You'll see more together. 9. Stay close to your customer Client's concerns evolve over the life of a project. Take advantage of that to over-deliver. Stay in a conversation with your client to adjust what you are doing.
cards.title: 10 Rules for Project Managers reference 1

cards.text: 8. Take care of your project team We've come to accept that the customer comes first ... the customer is always right. We can't take care of the customer if we first aren't taking care of our project team. It's a challenge. While there are some things we can do for the whole team, it comes down to taking care of each team member as the individual that he or she is. And to make it more difficult, then we must bring their various interests into coherence.
cards.title: 10 Rules for Project Managers reference 2

cards.text: 7. Keep your eye on the overall project promises Project work can be difficult. It is easy to loose sight of what we are doing and why we are doing it. Remind your team and yourself of the overall promises and how you are doing fulfilling those promises. 6. Build relationships intentionally Project teams come together as strangers. To do great work...innovation, learning, and collaboration...all take people who like and care for each other. Don't leave that to chance. Start your projects by building relationships among team members.
cards.title: 10 Rules for Project Managers reference 3

cards.text: 5. Tightly couple learning with action Projects are wonderful opportunities to learn. Don't put that off for the after project lessons learned. Make it your habit to incorporate learning loops in all your project activities. Your team will appreciate it. Your customer will benefit from it. And best of all, it will make your job easier. 4. Coordinate meticulously A project is an ever-evolving network of commitment. Keep that network activated by tending to the critical conversations. See that people are making clear requests, promises that have completion dates, and share opinions that advance the purposes of the project. Without attention to those critical conversations the project will drift.
cards.title: 10 Rules for Project Managers reference 4

cards.text: 3. Collaborate. Really collaborate. Make it your rule to plan with those people who will be the performers of the plan. Don't wait until the project has gone south to get their help. Start out that way. Continue collaborating as the usual way you work through the project. 2. Listen generously People are able to say what they can in the moment. For the most part, people are well-intended. Give them the benefit of the doubt. Take the time to listen. Ask questions. Seek others' opinions. And while you're at it, don't be so harsh on yourself.
cards.title: 10 Rules for Project Managers reference 5

cards.text: 1. Embrace uncertainty Expect the unexpected. There is far more that we don't know and can't know than what we can anticipate. Be resilient to what life throws at you. Anticipate that your team will learn something along the way that can and should change what you have promised and how you can deliver on your promises. And when you take a set-back -- we all do sometime or another -- review the other nine rules for how you can work your way out of it. From the web log of Hal Macomber - for more of Hal's PM wisdom, Google Hal Macomber or go to http://weblog.halmacomber.com/
cards.title: 10 Rules for Project Managers reference 6

Real Accountability Defining Accountabilities Directions: Work with your team to select the accountabilities best suited for each individual, the team, and the overall business. Use the GNA Accountability Tracking Spreadsheet (available for download in the course) to document your work. • Define major accountabilities for each person. • Give each person an opportunity to choose for themselves. • Every task is held within someone's accountability. Accountability: an opportunity to report-to account or to say what someone has done. They encompass every task performed in the company.
cards.title: 3 Steps to Power Academy Workbook reference 3

cards.text: Ensure that every action, task, and needed outcome in the whole business is assigned and held inside a specific accountability such as marketing, sales, business development, production, and or project management. Review and discuss each task thoroughly, ensuring clarity and alignment among all team members. Questions: • Did each person choose their own accountability with their team, or was it assigned to them? • Does the person holding each accountability have the right skills to execute successfully? • Did the people currently holding each accountability choose the whole of the accountability, including all the needed actions and results to be successful, or do they feel like some of it was forced on them?
cards.title: 3 Steps to Power Academy Workbook reference 4

cards.text: When ready, head back to the online course to learn more about How to Construct Reports. Reports Directions: Construct simple and clear reports for each participating team member. Follow these steps to ensure your reports are effective and transparent: • Construct a Report for Each Person: Design a report for each member of the team outlining the task/responsibility and results for each team member. • Keep It Simple and Clear: Focus on simplicity. Each report should be easy to read and understand, avoiding unnecessary details or complex formats. Aim for transparency so everyone can quickly see the key facts in one minute at most.
cards.title: 3 Steps to Power Academy Workbook reference 5

cards.text: • Highlight Results: The report should clearly show the metrics for results achieved. • Use Timeframes to Show Trends: Include past, present, and future data to give a clear picture of progress over time. This will help the team track trends and stay focused on long-term goals. Keep it simple; use a 3 or 4-month view. • Ensure visibility and transparency of Issues: If the reporting is clear, any breakdowns, issues, or challenges will be easily identifiable. This allows for faster problem-solving and course correction. By following these steps, your reports will keep everyone on the same page and empower the team to take ownership of their tasks, leading to greater success and alignment.
cards.title: 3 Steps to Power Academy Workbook reference 6

cards.text: Note: In the online course you will find a download: GNA Sample Reports.zip These are examples only. Please use the reports as a reference to guide and design your own reports. cards.text: What's In It For You: In this activity, you will identify key outcomes as opportunities to promise in your role. Directions: • Review Your Employee Evaluation Matrix  Reflect on the behaviors, attitudes, and performance you've observed in everyone. • Identify Next Steps for Coachable Employees  For each employee you've deemed coachable, identify specific actions you can take to reinforce their positive behaviors.

cards.text: This should include: • Make clear acknowledgments for specific accomplishments, results exceeding targets, and especially breakthroughs significantly exceeding targets. • Set new goals or challenges to take their performance to the next level. • Create a one-year plan with training and development goals to support their career path. Make it challenging yet doable. • Identify Next Steps for Uncoachable Employees For each employee you've deemed to have uncoachable behaviors, identify specific actions you can take to develop a clear exit strategy for them. Outline the following: • A timeline for addressing the issue with the employee/employees. This is a last-chance action to see if the employee becomes coachable.

cards.text: • List the necessary actions for transitioning them out of the business in a way that minimizes disruption. • Plan Your Conversations  Prepare for any conversations you'll need to have, whether it's a praise and development talk for coachable employees or an exit conversation for those who are uncoachable. Be clear and direct, ensuring that your communication aligns with your overall team goals. Note: If you still have problematic performance after completing the actions above, it may be one of two reasons. • Your coaching style isn't effective for that person. • The person you are coaching is uncoachable.

cards.text: In the next activity, you will align your leadership decisions with the needs of your business. cards.text: • If after having done this, you still have someone that is still challenged in achieving their goals … go to Advanced Coaching Tools for The Performance Challenged below. cards.text: In a one-on-one meeting with this person, quickly review steps 1-4. cards.text: The intent here is NOT to have them feel bad about themselves, but to have them feel responsible for the lack of results, offer the opportunity to look at what didn't work, and make corrections. In the same way, acknowledging each person for their positive results is empowering, and so is being clear, straight, and honest in acknowledging each person for what they aren't accomplishing, which is very empowering. You're dealing with fully grown adults, so it's okay to treat them as adults who are fully accountable for their responsibilities and accountabilities. This is a critically important component for a culture of continuous improvement. Warning!

cards.text: When you're ready, head back to the online course to learn more about Creating Coaching Breakthroughs. Coaching for a Culture of Breakthrough Performance "If you build it, they will come." field of dreams, 1989 Objective: Meet with each person in your team and establish an individualized coaching plan. cards.text: List your answers in the Action Plan tab. • Meet with each team member individually. The goal of these meetings is to: • Provide a completely transparent view of the results each person accomplishes inside their own accountability. • Allow each person to objectively see where they are now in relationship to their own next level of performance. • Offer the support, planning, and milestone actions needed for that person to realize their goals, overcome challenges, and identify areas where support is needed. Start by asking the following coaching questions. • List the area(s) do you need the most coaching or training?

cards.text: Create these together to ensure each person feels ownership of their goals and understands their responsibility, as well as the role that your coaching support will play in achieving them. • What do you need in terms of training and development? • Select, design, and plan the courses and training as needed. Whether it's online or requiring travel, or training that can be done in-house. • Annual, Monthly, Weekly Milestones: Start with what that person wants to achieve one year from now. Then, work backward to have monthly and possibly weekly milestones and key performance indicators (KPIs) that you both will use to support and measure their progress.

cards.text: These milestones and KPIs should be clear, challenging yet possible, and have timelines that are mutually agreed upon. • Tip: It's ok to be unreasonable and challenging in setting up what will be achieved one year out. Don't underestimate what people are capable of; they just might surprise you. Also, don't beat them up for going for it and not being successful. • Build The Support Plan: Schedule regular check-ins to track progress and adjust the coaching plan as needed. This could be through weekly or bi-weekly meetings to discuss challenges, celebrate wins, and continue providing support.

cards.text: • Reflection: After completing your meetings, reflect on how well you understood each person's needs and how effectively you were able to establish coaching goals. Document what went well and any adjustments you might need to make for future sessions. [What is the point of the key outcomes? We need to explain why this is here. It's the first time that has shown up in this guide] A long-lasting, successful business requires more than just a concern for being financially focused. Businesses are people, so to reach for the highest potential of your business, you need a methodology and structure for coaching each person in reaching for their highest potential.
cards.title: 3 Steps to Power Academy Workbook reference 42

cards.text: Key Outcomes: • You have a clear coaching plan for each member of your team. • Each person has a key role in creating the plan with their upline manager. • This establishes a culture where one-on-one coaching is a widely accepted and integral practice for every person and every team's success. • Every person and every team has a clear one-year future with clear, actionable goals and milestones that they feel ownership of, that puts them on track for a breakthrough in their own accomplishments and performance • Each person is inspired and excited about what they have done, and where they see themselves going.

cards.text: By fostering an environment where coaching is not just top-down but an ongoing, collaborative process, you now have an empowering, continuously improving, self-sustaining team. Congratulations! You've reached the end of the 3 Steps to Power Workbook!

cards.text: COMMUNICATION FOR ACTION "When people master enduring communication and leadership skills, you get Explosive Productivity". We define ownership as actively accepting accountability for overall business results and impact on people. When people behave as owners they no longer have a "wait and see" attitude, instead they accept full responsibility for proactively leading change and producing results. GNA builds leaders at all levels through a structured and proven three step process.
cards.title: Communication for Action reference 1

cards.text: Successful change starts at the top with the senior leadership group of a business unit or organization. You can't afford to accept anything less than a cohesive leadership group that collectively drives the process for building a Great Company. The actions of this group send a strong message to people throughout the company. Mastering authentic and sustainable leadership alignment skills are critical for developing a cohesive and effective senior group.
cards.title: Communication for Action reference 2

cards.text: What does the Emotional Intelligence of your key employees have to do how profitable you are? I first became aware of the idea of emotional intelligence when the buzz around Daniel Goleman's book hit the street in 1995. I have been wanting to write something on this for almost that long, because in working with teams and employees individually, I see over and over how important both cognitive and emotional intelligence is….as an example; "Its 9:45 am on a Tuesday and I am sitting in applicant interviews with a resigned business owner. Resigned because we are conducting interviews for a new project manager and he isn't happy with what we have seen so far.
cards.title: Emotional Intelligence of Your Key Employees reference 1

cards.text: We have seen 4 people already, number 4 just left, we have 2 more to go, and were looking at the clock just waiting to get this done. As each one left we had a brief 2 to 3 min conversation about how we might be able to make that applicant work, not realizing how our whole position was coming from settling for less than what we really needed and wanted. We didn't see our blind spot until….number 5 walks in and seriously gets my attention. I sit up straight. I am immediately enrolled by his smile, gait, posture, eye contact, and energy level.
cards.title: Emotional Intelligence of Your Key Employees reference 2

cards.text: As he sits down he slides me his resume. He hasn't even said more than his name and I already have a strong intuition this is our guy. I look over at the owner, and he's looking at me with a look on his face that tells me the applicant got his attention to. The next few minutes will be very interesting. We have over a million in sales about to go into WIP and we need a solid, authentic, grounded, and experienced person to run the work. Someone that we can count on no matter what….." Here is the challenge that I see over and over again.
cards.title: Emotional Intelligence of Your Key Employees reference 3

cards.text: How do you know, how do you discern that the person sitting in front of you is going to be that rock star performer you really want and need? We look at resumes, we talk with them on the phone, we ask questions, listen to their response, then we meet with them and see what they are like in person. Sometimes we have them solve some work related problem, or sometime we have them write up a proposal of their first 6 month to a year. It's becoming more common to test key position applicants for a personality test, and some of those tests include emotional intelligence indicators.
cards.title: Emotional Intelligence of Your Key Employees reference 4

cards.text: But at no time ever have I ever seen a test just for emotional intelligence. I have heard and participated in conversations regarding applicants skills, talents, etc, but rarely have I heard conversations about a applicants EI. The truth is, we hire based on skill set and experience, we sometimes consider their personality and character. But we rarely put together the fact that many of the needed professional skills live in the EI world. Like some of the following: SELF-AWARENESS - knowing one's emotions, strengths, weaknesses, drives, values and goals and recognize their impact on others while using gut feelings to guide decisions.
cards.title: Emotional Intelligence of Your Key Employees reference 5

cards.text: Have you ever had the project manager or estimator that gathers their self esteem by pleasing others? Next thing you know their margins are slipping because they give free work to the homeowners…but their customers love them. SELF-REGULATION - Manage or redirect one's disruptive emotions and impulses and adapt to changing circumstances. What about the key employee (PM, Estimator, etc) that has all the right skills and experience….but they can't get along with anyone. They blow up relationships with customers or team members. And it's always the another's fault. Another thing here is time management and scheduling of projects.
cards.title: Emotional Intelligence of Your Key Employees reference 6

cards.text: High functioning estimators and project managers have excellent time management and project management scheduling skills that allow them to expand their work load like an accordion when needed. If the estimator or manager doesn't have these skills, they get overwhelmed, and from their point of view that they have too much work, and you need to hire more people. Sound familiar? SOCIAL SKILL - Manage other's emotions to move people in the desired direction. EMPATHY - Recognize, understand, and consider people's feelings when making decisions. MOTIVATION - Motivate oneself and others to achieve for the sake of achievement.
cards.title: Emotional Intelligence of Your Key Employees reference 7

cards.text: I put these last three together because they are critically important for any key leader or manager who has one of more people reporting to them. The best performance, the kind of performance where employees are achieving their goals, exceeding their goals, and excited because they are having breakthroughs in their accomplishments, comes from a level of productivity that lives somewhere between people doing what they are inspired to do and what they are committed to do. Teams that reach that level of productivity are highly successful and highly profitable.
cards.title: Emotional Intelligence of Your Key Employees reference 8

cards.text: In order to support your teams in reaching the best of their potential, you need key managers as well as key employees who have these social, empathy, and motivation skills. This kind of intelligence allows for the kind of understanding, communication, and coaching with individuals to build on their existing skills, and unleash their potential. Without this, employees resist support, and experience education and empowerment as a threat. Managerial efforts typically fall to management by force, or management through fear of some kind of punitive action, or offers of financial reward. Best case…those management styles typically meet with marginal success, as long as the effort is maintained.
cards.title: Emotional Intelligence of Your Key Employees reference 9

cards.text: Worst case, owners and managers become frustrated, stressed, and exhausted. Bottom line is, if you want rock star employees, pay attention to their skills, experience, and their mood, energy level, ability to be coachable, capacity for learning, and willingness to give and keep their word on challenging outcomes and results. Ultimately, you want can do, I can make it happen, I will make it happen people. And those folks will have strong self esteem, self worth, and integrity, with the history of results to back that up.
cards.title: Emotional Intelligence of Your Key Employees reference 10

cards.text: I was meeting with a Contractor yesterday as we were reviewing his profit and loss and job cost spreadsheets, and I was reminded of how, no matter how many times we hear it, it bears repeating:
cards.title: Evaluate Performance reference 1

cards.text: Its not profit until it shows up in your net margin. When asked "Are you making money?" I have heard some really amazing methods of determining this, ranging from counting the monthly deposits in the register, to how many faxes requesting work come in every day, and how much money is left over at the end of the week after paying the crew… but the bottom line is you need to have a very accurate bookkeeping system, you have to know your margins better than you know your dog, and you have to trust your information to help you steer your business decisions.
cards.title: Evaluate Performance reference 2

cards.text: It may take a few weeks, or two or three months, but it is well worth the time it takes for you to have certainty about where you stand financially. Take the time to establish what the Key Performance Indicators are for your business. Minimally, start with your overhead, net, gross profit margins, and job costing. Design your office reporting systems to give you reliable, up-to-date information on at least a monthly basis. Many contractors doing under 1.5 million have part-time office staff, so it's even better if you can train that staff in helping to provide the information needed; otherwise they default to merely making the necessary data entry.
cards.title: Evaluate Performance reference 3

cards.text: Spend the time and the effort to go through all of your expenses every month. You will get out of this effort exactly what you put into it. If you guess at numbers, your budget will be a guess. If you really get in and do your homework, your budget will become your bible of expenses for the coming year. This is one of the key issues in getting out, or staying out, of debt. The most successful companies I know, no matter what their size, pay extremely close attention to every financial detail.
cards.title: Evaluate Performance reference 4

cards.text: Negative %: You need to get some help, and the sooner the better. The reality is that you are where you are based on decisions you and you alone have made. Things are not going to get any better, and will probably get worse unless you make some serious changes.

cards.text: If you are equating the success of your company to anything other than your bottom line; i.e., your quality of life, how happy your customers are, how many days off a week or vacations you take, the toys you have, you are kidding yourself. Those are the signs of a successful hobby. And please don't give tell me the tired old line, "I am not in business just for the money." Idealism will not feed your family or pay your bills.  Total sales for the year  # of phone calls into the company for the year  # of leads for the year  Sales to leads ratio (Closing ratio or %)  Average job size

cards.text: So, here's what you do, set up one person to be the driver accountable for this new hire project. NOT you, someone else. cards.text: If you were looking for a great company to work for would you want to respond to a boring, plain generic ad? It also needs to describe something about the culture of your business because the kind of person you really want to hire values a great place to work almost or as much as how much you'll be paying them.

cards.text: It also needs to say something towards what they will be accountable for, what is expected of them. And this is important - its needs to describe the challenge and the level of performance you really want. Often times due to believing you can't find good help and thinking it will be difficult to find a good person, you settle.

cards.text: Finding great people to work for you doesn't have to be hard. It can take time though and having an effective hiring process is crucially important to increasing your company's productivity and net profits. The most important part is reading every resume, and calling every single one that might be a possibility. You need to weed out the ones who are clearly not a good fit and call every single person who could be a possible a candidate to fill your position. I know it's more work to make all those calls, and schedule all those interviews, but it's important.

cards.text: Keep in mind working for you company is a great opportunity and something you shouldn't take for granted. You've worked hard to build your company and it's an honor for someone to work for and with you. You need to understand if you want great people, you must have a great hiring process in place. Here's what an effective hiring process could look like for you: Start with really good ad copy. Weed out the obviously bad resumes. cards.text: You'll want to do this because how a candidate sounds on the phone is often times very different than how they are in person In the Interview Process, have questions prepared that will allow the applicant to demonstrate their knowledge of what you will want them to do for you. How you do this from day one, the requests you make, the challenges you set up, are what will set you apart from the other companies.
